Persist the adapter choice by NET_LUID (a stable u64, IP_ADAPTER_ADDRESSES_LH.Luid / MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW.InterfaceLuid), NOT by ifIndex. Interface indices are reassigned across reboots, driver updates and adapter add/remove. Both GetIpInterfaceEntry and GetBestRoute2 accept a LUID directly.

TransmitLinkSpeed is u64::MAX (18446744073709551615) for every disconnected adapter — it must be rendered as 'unknown', never as '18446744073.7 Gbps'. Get-NetAdapter reports the same thing as '0 bps'. (Directly relevant to this user's standing market-data-honesty rule: do not display a number the OS did not actually supply.)

A WireGuard VPN adapter reports IfType 53 (PropVirtual), NOT 131 (Tunnel). Any 'is this a VPN?' heuristic keyed on IfType 131 will miss WireGuard entirely. Prefer checking whether the best-route interface is outside the user's two configured candidates.

IP_ADAPTER_ADDRESSES_LH requires 8-byte alignment. The obvious `vec![0u8; size]` buffer is only 1-byte aligned and casting it is UB (it happens to work until it doesn't). Allocate `Vec<u64>` of `size.div_ceil(8) + 1` words and cast that. The buffer must also outlive every pointer walked out of it — return it alongside the head pointer.

MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW.Metric is only honoured when UseAutomaticMetric is false. Setting Metric while UseAutomaticMetric stays true will silently do nothing. Conversely, restoring Windows' default behaviour means setting UseAutomaticMetric = true (Metric is then ignored), which is the correct 'reset' action rather than writing back a remembered number.

MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW's boolean fields are plain Rust `bool` in windows-rs 0.62.2 (not BOOL/BOOLEAN newtypes), so no `.as_bool()` / `.into()` dance is needed — but that also means they are 1 byte and any manual struct layout assumptions are wrong.

GetIpInterfaceEntry / SetIpInterfaceEntry / GetIpInterfaceTable / GetBestRoute2 return `Foundation::WIN32_ERROR`, a newtype over u32 — NOT a `windows::core::Result`. There is no `?` operator support; compare `rc.0 == 0`. GetAdaptersAddresses is different again and returns a bare `u32`. Mixing these up is the most likely early bug.

GetAdaptersAddresses' `family` parameter is a bare `u32` (pass `AF_UNSPEC.0 as u32`) while GetIpInterfaceTable's is a typed `ADDRESS_FAMILY` (pass `AF_INET`). The inconsistency is in the generated bindings, not in your code.
GAA_FLAG_SKIP_DNS_INFO is generated as a bare `u32` constant while every other GAA_FLAG_* is the `GET_ADAPTERS_ADDRESSES_FLAGS` newtype, so it cannot be OR'd with the others without a cast.
IN_ADDR's S_addr is already stored in network byte order in memory. Use `.to_ne_bytes()` to build an Ipv4Addr; `.to_be_bytes()` reverses the octets on x86 and yields a silently wrong address.

Matching an `IF_OPER_STATUS` against the generated `IfOperStatusUp`-style constants compiles but emits 'constant in pattern should have an upper case name' warnings — and worse, a typo'd constant name in a match arm becomes an irrefutable binding that silently swallows every value. Match on the `.0` i32 payload instead.

eframe 0.36 removed `App::update(&mut self, ctx: &Context, frame)`. Essentially every egui tutorial, blog post and StackOverflow answer online predates this and will not compile. The required method is `fn ui(&mut self, ui: &mut egui::Ui, frame: &mut Frame)`, and `CentralPanel::show` takes `&mut Ui` rather than `&Context`. There is also an optional `fn logic(&mut self, ctx, frame)` called before each `ui` (and while the window is hidden) — that is the right hook for polling interface state without doing UI work.

eframe's default features pull in wgpu: 14.3 MB binary, 422 crates. Switching to `default-features = false, features = ["glow", "default_fonts"]` gives 6.7 MB and 190 crates for an identical-looking widget. Dropping `default_fonts` too would break text rendering unless fonts are supplied.

A transparent window needs BOTH `.with_transparent(true)` on the ViewportBuilder AND an `App::clear_color` returning `Rgba::TRANSPARENT` — the builder flag alone leaves an opaque background painted by the renderer.

A borderless window (`with_decorations(false)`) has no titlebar, so it cannot be dragged by default. Add a full-surface `ui.interact(ui.max_rect(), id, Sense::click_and_drag())` and send `ViewportCommand::StartDrag` on `drag_started()`. Also add `.with_taskbar(false)` so the widget does not occupy a taskbar slot.

Ethernet on this machine is currently UNPLUGGED (OperStatus Down, Connected=false, only a 169.254.x.x APIPA address) yet GetIpInterfaceEntry still returns a valid Metric=5 row for it. That is good news — metrics are readable, and almost certainly writable, on a down interface — but it means 'has a metric' is not evidence of 'has connectivity'.

Windows' automatic metrics on this box are Ethernet=5 and Wi-Fi=30, so a 25-point gap already favours Ethernet. To force Wi-Fi to win, the Ethernet metric must be raised above 30; picking something like 9000 for the 'loser' is safer than a small delta, and stays below the 9999 practical ceiling.

The WcmSvc GroupPolicy key (which can force Windows to tear down Wi-Fi whenever Ethernet is present, defeating the whole product) does NOT exist on this machine, so nothing will fight the widget here. It should still be probed at runtime on other machines and surfaced as a warning — the value to look for is fMinimizeConnections.
open_questions: SetIpInterfaceEntry was deliberately never called (read-only mandate), so the write path is entirely unproven on this machine. Specifically unverified: whether it returns ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER unless SitePrefixLength is zeroed on a row obtained from GetIpInterfaceEntry (a widely reported MSDN trap), and whether it returns ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (5) rather than something else when run unelevated.

The actual traffic flip could not be observed: the Ethernet cable is unplugged right now, so Ethernet and Wi-Fi were never simultaneously Up. The core premise — that raising the metric on the connected Ethernet interface moves the default route to Wi-Fi while the link stays UP — remains untested end to end. This needs a re-run with the cable plugged in.
Whether metric changes take effect immediately or need a route-cache flush / brief settle time before GetBestRoute2 reports the new winner. Unknown; needs the plugged-in test.

Whether the ProtonVPN tunnel would keep winning even after Ethernet/Wi-Fi metrics change (near certain, given its metric 0), and what the widget should do about it — detect and warn, or offer to steer only the underlying physical path.

IPv6 was not exercised at all. The same steering almost certainly must be applied to AF_INET6 rows too, or traffic will split (v6 over one NIC, v4 over the other) on dual-stack networks. Needs a second GetIpInterfaceEntry/SetIpInterfaceEntry pass with Family = AF_INET6.

Task Scheduler registration (--install-tasks) and the unelevated-widget-triggers-elevated-task flow were not touched at all, per the no-scheduled-tasks constraint. The UAC-free trigger path is still unproven.

Whether the widget should restore UseAutomaticMetric = true on uninstall/exit versus writing back the previously observed numeric metric. Restoring the automatic flag is cleaner, but if the user had a hand-set metric before install (as vEthernet 39 and ProtonVPN 43 do here, both UseAutomaticMetric=false), that original intent would be destroyed. Needs a save/restore design decision.
tray-icon support was not tested; only the eframe viewport was. The tray icon crate choice and its interaction with eframe's winit event loop is unverified.
Whether `.with_taskbar(false)` behaves correctly on Windows 10 as well as Windows 11 — only tested on Windows 11 Education 26200.

verification.topic: Adversarial verification of the LinkSwitch PoC dive (windows-rs 0.62.2 IP Helper + eframe 0.36.1 borderless widget)

refuted.claim: 'The WcmSvc GroupPolicy key that can block simultaneous Ethernet+Wi-Fi connections is NOT present on this machine, so no policy will fight the widget here.' (source: Get-ItemProperty -> 'NO SUCH KEY')
refuted.why_wrong:
Wrong on both halves, and the second half is a product-premise threat.

(a) The key EXISTS. Verified read-only: Test-Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WcmSvc\GroupPolicy' => True; Get-Item => ValueCount=0, SubKeyCount=0. The sibling 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WcmSvc\Local' holds WCMPresent=REG_DWORD 0x1. Their probe used `Get-ItemProperty <key> -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`, which emits NOTHING for a key that exists with zero values -- so their script printed 'NO SUCH KEY' for an empty-but-present key. That exact probe logic, shipped as the runtime warning, will misreport on every machine.

(b) Far worse: an absent fMinimizeConnections does NOT mean the behaviour is off. learn.microsoft.com/windows-hardware/drivers/mobilebroadband/understanding-and-configuring-windows-connection-manager, verbatim: 'This policy is configured by using the fMinimizeConnections Group Policy. The policy is on by default for Windows 8, Windows 8.1, and Windows 10.' Default == the enum value 1: 'any new automatic internet connection is blocked when the computer has at least one active internet connection to a preferred type of network. The order of preference is as follows: 1. Ethernet 2. WLAN 3. Cellular. Ethernet is always preferred when connected. Users can still manually connect to any network.' Remaining networks are soft-disconnected: 'As soon as Windows decides to soft-disconnect an interface, it informs the TCP stack that the network should no longer be used... Windows checks the traffic level on the interface every 30 seconds... When the traffic drops below the threshold, the interface is disconnected.' The dive read the missing registry value as 'safe' when it actually means 'stock default, i.e. Windows is actively trying to tear down Wi-Fi while Ethernet is connected' -- exactly the product's operating state.
refuted.correction: Probe the VALUE, not the key: read REG_DWORD fMinimizeConnections under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\WcmSvc\GroupPolicy and treat value-missing as ENABLED (=1), not disabled. Only an explicit 0 means 'simultaneous connections permitted, traffic routable over either'. Values: 0 = simultaneous allowed; 1 = block new automatic internet connections when a more-preferred type is up (legacy 'Enabled'); 2 = as 1 plus cellular kept alive; 3 = as 2 plus users may not even manually connect WLAN while Ethernet is present. Note 3 would hard-break the product. Mitigations for the widget: (i) the doc says maintained networks include 'Any networks manually connected during the current user session', so a user-initiated Wi-Fi connection survives; (ii) the elevated installer can offer to write fMinimizeConnections=0; (iii) surface it in the UI rather than letting Wi-Fi silently vanish ~30 s after traffic quiesces. Also note 'Windows responds to Ethernet connections but doesn't automatically manage Ethernet connections' -- the cable side is safe, only Wi-Fi gets torn down, which is the direction that hurts.

refuted.claim: 'Windows default interface metrics on this machine follow the documented auto-metric-by-speed table: 1Gbps+ Ethernet = 5, Wi-Fi = 30 ... so raising the loser above the winner needs a delta of at least 25 to flip Ethernet-vs-WiFi' (and the derived gotcha 'a 25-point gap already favours Ethernet')
refuted.why_wrong:
There is no '1 Gbps+ Ethernet = 5' row in any Microsoft table. KB299540 (learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/windows-server/networking/automatic-metric-for-ipv4-routes) publishes THREE tables; only the Windows-10-and-later pair applies, and it splits wireless from everything else. 'Other interfaces': >=100 Gb->5, >=40<100 Gb->10, >=10<40 Gb->15, >=2<10 Gb->20, >=200 Mb<2 Gb->25, >=80<200 Mb->35, >=20<80 Mb->45, >=4<20 Mb->55, >=500 Kb<4 Mb->65, <500 Kb->75.

The observed Ethernet=5 is an artifact of the cable being OUT. My own run of their code prints for ifIndex 4: TransmitLinkSpeed = 18446744073709551615 (u64::MAX, 'unknown'), which lands in the top bucket >=100 Gb -> 5. Independent confirmation on the same box: the two Wi-Fi Direct virtual adapters (16, 17) also report u64::MAX and get metric 25 -- the top bucket of the WIRELESS table. Every adapter with a real link speed matches its documented bucket exactly: Wi-Fi 1.201 Gbps halved for half-duplex per the KB ('For half-duplex interfaces, such as wireless, the effective speed is half of the advertised speed') = 600 Mb -> wireless >=500 Mb <2 Gb -> 30; VMware 100 Mb -> 35; Bluetooth 3 Mb -> 65. So the table does fit -- but it fits in a way that refutes the conclusion drawn from it.

Consequence: the instant the user plugs the cable in (the only state this product ever runs in), the 2.5 GbE Intel I225-V leaves the 'unknown' bucket and lands in '>= 2 Gb and less than 10 Gb' = 20, against Wi-Fi's 30. The real gap is 10, not 25. On a 1 GbE link it would be 25 vs 30, a gap of 5. And Wi-Fi's metric moves continuously as the 802.11 rate negotiates (the RZ608 will cross the 500 Mb effective boundary and jump 30 <-> 35 on its own).
refuted.correction: Never precompute or hardcode a delta -- the number the dive measured belongs to the cable-unplugged state. At apply time: read the CURRENT MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW.Metric of both candidates (for both AF_INET and AF_INET6), then set the loser to a fixed high constant with UseAutomaticMetric=false and restore the winner to UseAutomaticMetric=true (Metric ignored). Re-read after applying and verify the ordering actually inverted rather than assuming it. Expect Ethernet's automatic metric to change value on cable plug/unplug -- treat 'Ethernet metric == 5' as a strong hint the link is DOWN, not that it is fast.

refuted.claim: 'Choosing glow over the default wgpu roughly halves the binary and cuts the dependency graph by more than half: 6,717,440 bytes / 190 deps vs 14,312,960 bytes / 422 deps (release)' (source: cargo tree | wc -l)
refuted.why_wrong:
190 and 422 are `cargo tree` OUTPUT LINES, not crates. cargo tree prints a crate once per edge in the graph, so shared dependencies are counted many times over. Measured on this machine with the same two Cargo.tomls: `cargo tree -e normal --prefix none | sed 's/ (\*)//' | awk 'NF' | sort -u | wc -l` gives glow = 96 unique crates, wgpu = 167. The dive's numbers are inflated ~2x and the ratio is wrong too (they claim 'more than half' cut; it is 96/167 = 43% fewer).

The binary figure is also measured under a profile the dive does not itself recommend: their own guipoc_glow finished in 34.79 s, which cannot be an lto=true, codegen-units=1 build. With the exact [profile.release] from their own recommended linkswitch Cargo.toml (opt-level='z', lto=true, codegen-units=1, strip=true) the glow build took 1m13s and produced 5,911,040 bytes, not 6,717,440.
refuted.correction: Use glow -- the recommendation is right, the arithmetic is not. Correct figures for the brief: 96 crates vs 167 crates; glow release with the size profile = 5.9 MB. Report unique-crate counts, not cargo tree line counts. (I did not build the wgpu variant -- its 14.3 MB figure is unverified and was measured under the same unclear profile.)

refuted.claim: Code snippet: `let rc = unsafe { GetBestRoute2(None, 0, None, &dest, 0, &mut best, &mut best_src) };` presented as the verified way to ask 'who wins?'
refuted.why_wrong: It violates the documented contract. learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/api/netioapi/nf-netioapi-getbestroute2 Remarks, verbatim: 'On input, the DestinationAddress parameter must be initialized to a valid IPv4 or IPv6 address and family... In addition, at least one of the following parameters must be initialized: the InterfaceLuid or InterfaceIndex.' The snippet passes InterfaceLuid=None AND InterfaceIndex=0 -- neither is initialized. I reproduced that it returns NO_ERROR and if=43 on this machine, so it 'works', but it is relying on undocumented behaviour for the one call the whole status indicator hangs off.
refuted.correction: Always pin an interface, which is also the dive's own remedy for the VPN problem -- so there is no reason to keep the unpinned form anywhere. Call GetBestRoute2 once per candidate with `interfaceluid: Some(&luid)`; the LUID is used first and InterfaceIndex only if the LUID is zero. MSDN also documents the source-address route: 'If a source IP address is specified in the route lookup using GetBestRoute2... the route lookup is restricted to the interface of the source IP address' (MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW Remarks) -- passing sourceaddress = that adapter's unicast IP is the first-party way to get a per-interface answer under the strong host model.

refuted.claim: Open question / code comment: 'KNOWN MSDN TRAP: SitePrefixLength must be reset before Set or the call fails with ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER on rows returned by Get' -- listed as widely-reported folklore and explicitly unverified
refuted.why_wrong:
Not folklore, and not unverified any more -- but also not unconditional, and the dive's own IPv6 open question would have applied it wrongly. It is documented and it is IPv4-ONLY. SetIpInterfaceEntry Remarks, verbatim (twice): 'However for IPv4, an application must not try to modify the SitePrefixLength member of the MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW structure. For IPv4, the SitePrefixLength member must be set to 0.' MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW docs: 'For an IPv4 address, any value greater than 32 is an illegal value.'

I verified the precondition empirically WITHOUT ever calling Set: my rebuild of their reader prints SitePrefixLength for every row, and GetIpInterfaceEntry returns SitePrefixLength = 64 for every AF_INET interface on this machine (ifIndex 1, 4, 6, 14, 16, 17, 19, 23). 64 > 32 = illegal, so the zeroing is mandatory, not defensive. Supporting evidence: the only two rows that read back SitePrefixLength = 0 are ifIndex 43 (ProtonVPN) and 39 (vEthernet) -- precisely the two with UseAutomaticMetric=false, i.e. the two that something already wrote via SetIpInterfaceEntry.
refuted.correction: Keep `row.SitePrefixLength = 0;` for the AF_INET pass -- it is required, not optional. Do NOT blanket-copy it into the AF_INET6 pass the dive's open questions call for: the MSDN rule is IPv4-specific (IPv6 legal range is <=128), so for AF_INET6 carry through whatever GetIpInterfaceEntry returned. Also note SetIpInterfaceEntry outright IGNORES MaxReassemblySize, Min/MaxRouterAdvertisementInterval, Connected, SupportsWakeUpPatterns, SupportsNeighborDiscovery, SupportsRouterDiscovery, ReachableTime, TransmitOffload, ReceiveOffload -- 'These members are set by the network stack and cannot be changed' -- so no save/restore effort is needed for any of them.

added_gotchas: USE MIB_IF_ROW2 FLAGS TO PICK THE TWO PHYSICAL NICS -- there is a clean first-party answer and the dive proposed a fragile APIPA heuristic instead. On this machine `Get-NetAdapter -IncludeHidden` lists 22 adapters; HardwareInterface=True AND ConnectorPresent=True is true for EXACTLY two: ifIndex 4 (Ethernet) and ifIndex 14 (Wi-Fi). Every distractor the dive worried about -- both Wi-Fi Direct virtuals (16, 17), VMware VMnet1/8 (23, 19), Hyper-V vEthernet (39), Bluetooth PAN (6), ProtonVPN (43) -- is HardwareInterface=False, ConnectorPresent=False, Virtual=True. API: windows::Win32::NetworkManagement::IpHelper::GetIfEntry2(row: *mut MIB_IF_ROW2) -> WIN32_ERROR, gated by Win32_NetworkManagement_Ndis ONLY (verified at IpHelper/mod.rs:386, no WinSock needed). CAUTION: windows-rs 0.62.2 generates the bitfield as `pub struct MIB_IF_ROW2_0 { pub _bitfield: u8 }` (IpHelper/mod.rs:2743) with NO accessor methods -- decode by hand. MSDN declaration order (LSB first): bit0 HardwareInterface, bit1 FilterInterface, bit2 ConnectorPresent, bit3 NotAuthenticated, bit4 NotMediaConnected, bit5 Paused, bit6 LowPower, bit7 EndPointInterface. So `hardware = f & 1 != 0`, `connector = f & 4 != 0`, `media_down = f & 16 != 0`. Bonus: MIB_IF_ROW2.PhysicalMediumType == NdisPhysicalMediumNative802_11 (9) or NdisPhysicalMediumWirelessLan (1) is a better 'is this Wi-Fi?' test than IfType 71 -- it is the same discriminator KB299540 says Windows itself uses to choose the wireless auto-metric table.

GetAdaptersAddresses NEEDS A RETRY LOOP, NOT TWO PASSES. The dive's `adapters()` sizes once, allocates, calls once more, and returns None on any non-zero rc. If an adapter appears between the two calls (VPN connecting, Wi-Fi Direct spinning up, VMware service starting -- all live on this box) the second call returns ERROR_BUFFER_OVERFLOW again and the widget silently shows nothing. MSDN's own guidance is to loop: re-read the size and retry ~3 times before giving up. Cheap fix, and the failure it prevents is exactly the kind that only shows up on a user's machine.

DON'T HAND-ROLL THE ERROR CONSTANTS. The dive declares `const ERROR_BUFFER_OVERFLOW: u32 = 111;` and `const NO_ERROR_U32: u32 = 0;`. windows::Win32::Foundation already has them, transitively available with no extra feature (Win32_NetworkManagement_IpHelper -> Win32_NetworkManagement -> Win32 -> Win32_Foundation, per windows-0.62.2/Cargo.toml lines 376/416/471/475): ERROR_BUFFER_OVERFLOW = WIN32_ERROR(111), NO_ERROR = WIN32_ERROR(0), ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED = WIN32_ERROR(5), ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER = WIN32_ERROR(87), ERROR_NOT_FOUND = WIN32_ERROR(1168), ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND = WIN32_ERROR(2). WIN32_ERROR derives PartialEq, so compare `rc == NO_ERROR` for the WIN32_ERROR-returning calls and `rc == ERROR_BUFFER_OVERFLOW.0` for GetAdaptersAddresses (bare u32). All six are worth handling: SetIpInterfaceEntry's documented failure set is exactly ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED / ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND / ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER / ERROR_NOT_FOUND.

NO Debug DERIVE ON ANY OF THE NETWORK STRUCTS. In windows 0.62.2, MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW (mod.rs:2966), MIB_IPFORWARD_ROW2 and IP_ADAPTER_ADDRESSES_LH derive only `Clone, Copy` plus a hand-written `impl Default { core::mem::zeroed() }`. `println!("{:?}", row)` will not compile -- print fields individually. NET_LUID_LH is a UNION (`{ Value: u64, Info: NET_LUID_LH_0 { _bitfield: u64 } }`, Ndis/mod.rs:2477) with no Debug/PartialEq/Hash either, so persisting the adapter choice by LUID means an unsafe `luid.Value` read and comparing raw u64s. Real LUIDs from this box, for test fixtures: Ethernet(4)=0x6008000000000, Wi-Fi(14)=0x47008000000000.

schtasks /Run CANNOT PASS ARGUMENTS -- this breaks the `--apply ethernet|wifi|auto` trigger design as literally stated. Verified from its own usage text on this machine: `SCHTASKS /Run [/S system [/U username [/P [password]]]] [/I] /TN taskname [/HRESULT] [/?]`. There is no parameter for action arguments. Options: (a) register THREE tasks with the argument baked into each action (LinkSwitch-Ethernet / LinkSwitch-WiFi / LinkSwitch-Auto) -- simplest and keeps the elevated worker argument-driven; or (b) use Task Scheduler 2.0 COM IRegisteredTask::RunEx with $(Arg0) substitution in the action's Arguments. The 'elevated worker reads config' variant works too, but then an unelevated process writes the input to an elevated HIGHEST-run-level process -- design that file's ACL deliberately rather than dropping it in %APPDATA%.

ELEVATION NEEDS A MANIFEST, NOT JUST A HIGHEST-RUN-LEVEL TASK. SetIpInterfaceEntry Remarks, verbatim: 'can only be called by a user logged on as a member of the Administrators group. If SetIpInterfaceEntry is called by a user that is not a member of the Administrators group, the function call will fail and ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED is returned. This function can also fail because of user account control (UAC)... this call will fail unless the application has been marked in the manifest file with a requestedExecutionLevel set to requireAdministrator.' The single-binary design means the SAME exe is both the unelevated widget and the elevated worker -- a requireAdministrator manifest on that binary would force a UAC prompt on the widget itself, defeating the whole point. Verify early whether a Task Scheduler HIGHEST run level alone satisfies the API without the manifest; if it does not, the worker has to be a second exe. This is the highest-risk untested assumption left in the plan, above the metric write itself.

METRIC WRITES ARE PERSISTENT -- a crash mid-switch leaves the machine steered forever. netsh exposes `store=active|persistent` (confirmed in `netsh interface ipv4 set interface /?` on this box); SetIpInterfaceEntry has no store parameter and writes the persistent configuration, the same one the 'Automatic metric' checkbox drives. Evidence on this machine: ifIndex 43 and 39 have carried UseAutomaticMetric=false across reboots. Design the worker to be idempotent and to write BOTH interfaces on every apply, and make 'restore' set UseAutomaticMetric=true (Metric is then ignored) rather than writing back a remembered number. Corroborating first-party line, from the Set-NetIPInterface docs: '-InterfaceMetric ... If this parameter value is set, then the AutomaticMetric parameter is automatically disabled.' Separately: `metric` still appears in netsh's Parameters list but is GONE from its Usage syntax line on this Windows 11 build -- do not plan on netsh as the fallback path; use Set-NetIPInterface or the API.

THE 9999 CEILING IS UNSOURCED. The dive advises 'picking something like 9000 ... stays below the 9999 practical ceiling.' I reflected the cmdlet's parameter metadata: Set-NetIPInterface -InterfaceMetric is plain System.UInt32 with NO ValidateRangeAttribute at all, and the published docs give no maximum. MIB_IPINTERFACE_ROW.Metric is ULONG. This machine already runs vEthernet(39) at 5000. Pick a high constant because it is comfortably above any auto-metric bucket (max published bucket is 85), not because of a ceiling that does not appear to exist.

MORE 'UNKNOWN' SENTINELS BEYOND TransmitLinkSpeed -- relevant to the standing market-data-honesty rule. Loopback (ifIndex 1) reports NlMtu = 4294967295 (u32::MAX) from BOTH GetIpInterfaceEntry and Get-NetIPInterface. And Get-NetIPInterface's InterfaceMetric for ifIndex 43 is genuinely $null, not 0 -- I confirmed `$null -eq $r.InterfaceMetric` is True, while netsh and the native API both report 0. Do not use Get-NetIPInterface as the oracle in tests; netsh interface ipv4 show interfaces agrees with the native API and is the better cross-check.

FIRST-PARTY ENDORSEMENT OF THE CHOSEN MECHANISM, worth quoting in the README. Windows Connection Manager doc: 'If a connected interface isn't in the process of being soft-disconnected, Windows determines the route by the metric in the routing table. If the route metric isn't specified manually, Windows automatically assigns a route metric based on the link speed of the adapter... If both are connected, the user or a desktop app can change route metrics to influence routing preferences.' Also note the caveat that qualifies the whole indicator: route preference is documented as interface metric PLUS MIB_IPFORWARD_ROW2.Metric (the per-route offset), so comparing two interface metrics is only valid while both 0.0.0.0/0 routes carry the same offset -- which happens to be true here (both 0) but is not guaranteed on a user's machine. Read MIB_IPFORWARD_ROW2.Metric too and compare the sums.

REPRODUCTION ARTIFACTS. I rebuilt and re-ran both PoCs verbatim rather than trusting the transcript; both compile warning-free on rustc 1.96.1 and the network one runs read-only (no Set* call was ever made, no registry or scheduled-task write). Network probe: C:\Users\FABRIZ~1\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\c--dev-ProjectPrometheus\2ad8e8e2-7365-4b74-a530-cfedb9a45581\scratchpad\netpoc (its src/main.rs also compiles the untested set_metric write path, so the write-side types are proven even though the call is never made; it additionally prints SitePrefixLength, which is what exposed the 64-vs-0 finding). Widget: ...\scratchpad\guipoc (glow) and ...\scratchpad\guipoc_wgpu (dep-count comparison only, not built).
verification.verdict: Trustworthy on the Rust and API layer, not trustworthy on Windows behaviour. Everything mechanical checks out: I re-derived the cfg gating straight from windows-0.62.2 source, rebuilt both PoCs verbatim (warning-free), re-ran the network probe read-only, and confirmed the crate versions against the crates.io API. The three-feature list, the WIN32_ERROR-vs-u32 return split, the plain-bool struct fields, the ADDRESS_FAMILY inconsistency, the GAA_FLAG_SKIP_DNS_INFO wart, and -- surprisingly, since it contradicts every tutorial -- the eframe 0.36 `fn ui(&mut self, &mut Ui, &mut Frame)` break and `CentralPanel::show(&mut Ui)` are all real. The VPN discovery is real and reproduces via Find-NetRoute independently. Build on that layer as written. But both of the dive's Windows-behaviour conclusions are wrong in the same direction -- each was inferred from a single observation of a machine in the wrong state, and each undercuts the product premise. (1) The auto-metric reading is an artifact of the unplugged cable: Ethernet's 5 is the 'link speed unknown' top bucket, not a fast-Ethernet value, and plugging in makes it 20 against Wi-Fi's 30. The '25-point gap' planning number belongs to the one state LinkSwitch never operates in. (2) The WCM claim has the polarity inverted: the key does exist, and more importantly a missing fMinimizeConnections means the minimize-connections behaviour is ON by default, so stock Windows is already trying to soft-disconnect Wi-Fi ~30 s after traffic quiesces whenever Ethernet is up.
